title: Seared duck breast with cherry sauce

notes.text: For more than 4, render the duck in two skillets, and roast all the breasts together on one sheet pan.

move.title: Score, render, sauce
move.body: A French bistro classic: duck breasts scored through the skin, started in a cold pan, and cooked slowly skin side down until the fat melts away and the skin turns thin and crisp. The fat is saved to roast potatoes, and the pan becomes a cherry and balsamic sauce, reduced until glossy. The duck is sliced thin across the grain.

why.title: Score the skin, not the meat
why.body: Duck skin sits on a thick layer of fat. A crosshatch cut 1 centimeter apart, through the skin and fat but not into the meat, lets the fat run out as it melts and keeps the skin from curling.

why.title: Start in a cold pan
why.body: A cold pan heats slowly, so the fat melts out before the skin browns. Started in a hot pan, the skin burns while the fat underneath stays thick and chewy.

why.title: Save the fat
why.body: Rendered duck fat is clean-tasting and stands up to high heat. Pour it off as it collects, into a heatproof bowl, and roast the potatoes in it.

why.title: Duck at 165°F
why.body: Restaurants often serve duck breast pink, at about 135°F. This app follows the USDA standard for all poultry, 165°F, so the breast finishes in the oven and is sliced thin to keep it tender.

why.title: Reduce to a glaze
why.body: Simmering the broth, balsamic, and cherries drives off water and concentrates the sugar and acid. It's ready when it coats the back of a spoon and a line drawn through it holds.

why.title: Slice across the grain
why.body: Duck breast fibers run lengthwise. Thin slices across them, on a slight angle, are tender even when the meat is cooked through.

wrong.sign: The skin is thick and rubbery
wrong.fix: It needed more time over low heat. Return it skin side down and keep rendering.

wrong.sign: The skin burned before the fat rendered
wrong.fix: The heat was too high. Turn it to medium-low and pour off the fat more often.
Stir in a teaspoon of honey, or a little more butter.

choices: So the fat can run out and the skin stays flat
quiz.explain: Cut the skin and fat, not the meat.

quiz.q: Why start duck in a cold pan?
choices: The fat melts out before the skin browns

quiz.q: What temperature does this app cook duck to?

steps.text: Heat the oven to 400°F with a rack in the middle.
Halve the potatoes and put them on the sheet pan.
Pat the duck dry. Score the skin in a crosshatch 1 centimeter apart, through the fat but not into the meat. Season both sides with the duck's salt and pepper.
steps.look: A diamond pattern; no red meat showing in the cuts.

steps.text: Throw the paper towels away. Wash your hands, the knife, and the board with hot, soapy water.
Lay the breasts skin side down in the cold skillet with the tongs. Set it over medium-low heat.
Wash the tongs and your hands.
Render without moving, pouring the fat into the heatproof bowl every 5 minutes, until the skin is thin and deep golden.
steps.look: Thin, crisp, mahogany skin; most of the fat gone.
steps.tip: Tilt the pan away from you to pour, and spoon the fat out if the pan is heavy.

steps.text: Toss the potatoes with 2 tablespoons of the duck fat and the potatoes' salt, and roast cut side down.
Turn the breasts and sear the meat side, then move them, skin side up, to the edge of the potato pan to finish in the oven.
Check the thickest breast: at least 165°F. If not, roast 2 minutes more.
Rest the duck on the board, skin side up.
Pour off all but 1 tablespoon of fat from the skillet. Mince the onion and cook it over medium heat until soft, then add the thyme, broth, balsamic, cherries, and honey.
Simmer until the sauce coats a spoon. Turn off the heat, swirl in the butter, and season with the sauce's salt.
steps.look: Glossy; a line drawn through it on the spoon holds.

steps.text: Slice the duck 5 millimeters thick across the grain, on a slight angle.
Fan the slices on plates with the potatoes and spoon the cherry sauce over.
